Adam: My friend Kristi just got a job as an editorial assistant at BFP, and she said there might be another position available. She said I was a shoo-in, but the job that she talked about is no longer posted on the company website.
Hayley: Oh, that's too bad. Maybe they will upload another position. Why don't you contact a headhunter in the field? I know someone. His name is Andrew Goldstein. He may be able tell you who is hiring and which companies are the best ones to work for.
Adam: OK, he might be able to help me. I'll write to him now.

Dear Mr. Goldstein,

Allow me to introduce myself. My name is Adam Bari. Ms. Hayley Sanders, who is my friend, suggested that I write to you. Perhaps I could benefit from your services. I reckon you have helped many people like me in the past.

I would be very interested in working in the area of communications. I am a recent graduate in the field. I imagine you have seen from my résumé that I worked as a copy editor and a proofreader at a campus newspaper, where I also sold advertising space. I am very interested in positions such as web content editor, editorial assistant or copy editor.

I take great pride in my writing style. I suppose you have thought of ways of promoting a candidate's written work. I have established a substantial portfolio of written work that you may be interested in viewing. I look forward to talking to you further about employment opportunities in communications, and how you could assist me with my job search.

Sincerely,

Adam Bari

Present Perfect with Comment Verbs or Phrases
You can use the Present Perfect with verbs like reckon, imagine and suppose when you want to comment or report on what has been done.

When you use the Present Perfect, you refer to things that happened in the past but have a connection to the present. This is useful when you talk about how things affect you and your current situation.

For example:

I reckon you have met many people like me.

I imagine you have seen from my résumé that I worked as a copy editor and proofreader at a campus newspaper, where I also sold advertising space.

I suppose you have established a portfolio of your written work.
The past participle of the main verb must be used in the Present Perfect tense.</br></br>  Look at the chart for the past participles of some verbs:

Modals to Express True and Untrue in the Present Tense
Modals are helping verbs. They add meaning to the main verbs of a sentence. They help  convey the speaker's intentions, feelings and attitudes toward a topic.
Common modals you hear in business settings are:  </br></br>could </br> might</br>  may

Perhaps I could benefit from your services.

You use the modal could to express possibility in both the past and present.

For example:

I could help you build your network of contacts and give you strategies for building your online presence.

You use the modal would to create conditional verb forms. It also serves as the past form of the modal verb "will."

For example:

I would be very interested in working in the area of communications.

You use might and may to express certainty about past and present actions or events.

For example:

He may be able to tell you who is hiring and which companies are the best ones to work for.
